warmup.q: Two MongoDB transactions run at the same time. Both read A-1001's balance of 100.00 and both try to debit it. The second debit is sent while the first transaction is still open. What happens to the second transaction?
options: It waits until the first one commits, then debits the new balance
Its debit fails at once with a write conflict, and the whole transaction has to run again
Both debits apply, and the balance ends up wrong
It succeeds, and the first transaction is aborted instead
warmup.why: MongoDB lets the first writer of a document win and fails the second write at once with WriteConflict, labelled TransientTransactionError. It doesn't queue it, because its snapshot is already stale: it read 100.00, which is no longer true. The fix is to abort and rerun the whole transaction on a new snapshot. Waiting is what a plain write outside any transaction does when it hits a document an open transaction has changed.

sections.h: DynamoDB runs lesson 7's two-phase commit, with a ledger any coordinator can finish
sections.html:
Lesson 7 built two-phase commit on PostgreSQL and found its weak spot: a coordinator whose crash leaves participants in doubt, holding locks, until it comes back with its log. NoSQL stores that offer transactions across partitions face exactly the same problem, because their partitions live on different machines. Each one answers the same three questions differently: who decides, what a participant promises, and where the decision lives. DynamoDB first.

In the Data models track's DynamoDB lesson, one TransactWriteItems debited A-1001, credited A-2002 and claimed an idempotency key, and DynamoDB applied all of it or none of it. It cost two writes per item and could fail with TransactionConflict. The scope is fixed: up to 100 actions on distinct items, 4 MB in all, in one account and one Region. In a global table the guarantee holds only in the Region where you wrote, and DynamoDB Streams don't keep the transaction together. A transaction is serializable against single-item reads and writes, but Query, Scan and BatchGetItem read it as read committed: a Query can see some of its items and not others. The client token makes a retry idempotent for 10 minutes.

How it works is in DynamoDB's 2023 USENIX paper, and it is lesson 7's protocol with the weak spot removed. Any coordinator in a large fleet can take a transaction, and it stamps the transaction with a timestamp from its clock. Phase one: a storage node accepts a prepare only if the item's condition holds, the timestamp is newer than the item's last write, and no other transaction is in flight on the item. That last rule replaces lock waits: a held item makes the node say no at once, and one no cancels the whole transaction. The coordinator records its decision in a ledger, itself a DynamoDB table, replicated like any other, before it sends the commits. If a coordinator dies, a recovery manager scanning the ledger hands its transaction to another coordinator, which finishes it. So nobody waits for one particular machine to come back, and no item stays held for long.

Atomic across machines still means every participant first promises, one decision is written where a crash can't erase it, and only then does anything change. The facts from the DynamoDB lesson fall out of this: two writes per item are the two rounds, and TransactionConflict is a rejected prepare. Transactions whose items all share one partition skip the protocol, because one node decides alone.

try.title: Run the two-phase protocol, with a conflict and a crash
steps: DynamoDB Local runs transactions one at a time, so it can't show a conflict: I sent it 20 concurrent three-item transfers out of one account, and all 20 committed on the first try. This demo runs the protocol from the paper as a small model instead. No Docker needed.

Read TwoPhaseDemo.kt. Before you run it, predict: which of T2's two prepares fails, and does A-3003's node keep anything from T2? In the second part, what happens to T4 while T3's coordinator is dead?
Run it from the labs folder, then check the final total: no money may appear or disappear.

code.title: TwoPhaseDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.txn.l08.demo /** One item with the metadata a DynamoDB storage node keeps next to it: its last write and the transaction preparing it. */ private class Item(val key: String, var balance: Long) { var lastWrite = 0L var ongoing: String? = null } /** One action of a transaction: change [key] by [delta], if [condition] holds on the current balance. */ private class Action(val key: String, val delta: Long, val condition: (Long) -> Boolean = { true }) private class Tx(val id: String, val timestamp: Long, val actions: List<Action>) /** * A model of the two-phase protocol in "Distributed Transactions at Scale in Amazon DynamoDB" * (USENIX ATC 2023): a coordinator prepares every item, then commits or cancels. Each item lives * on its own storage node, as if in its own partition. DynamoDB Local runs transactions one at a * time, so it can't show a conflict; this model can. */ fun main() { val items = listOf(Item("A-1001", 10_000), Item("A-2002", 5_000), Item("A-3003", 0)).associateBy { it.key } val ledger = mutableMapOf<String, String>() // the coordinators' durable record: transaction id -> decision fun log(tx: String, what: String) = println("%-3s %s".format(tx, what)) /** Phase 1 on one item: the checks from the paper's prepare listing. */ fun prepare(tx: Tx, a: Action): Boolean { val item = items.getValue(a.key) val verdict = when { item.ongoing != null -> "REJECTED: ${item.ongoing} is in flight on this item" tx.timestamp <= item.lastWrite -> "REJECTED: older than the item's last write" !a.condition(item.balance) -> "REJECTED: condition failed (balance ${item.balance})" else -> null } log(tx.id, "prepare ${a.key}: ${verdict ?: "accepted"}") if (verdict == null) item.ongoing = tx.id // the item is now held for this transaction return verdict == null } fun commit(tx: Tx) { for (a in tx.actions) { val item = items.getValue(a.key) val before = item.balance item.balance += a.delta item.lastWrite = tx.timestamp item.ongoing = null log(tx.id, "commit ${a.key}: $before -> ${item.balance}") } ledger[tx.id] = "COMPLETED" } /** One coordinator running one transaction. [crashBeforeCommit] stops it after it has decided. */ fun run(tx: Tx, crashBeforeCommit: Boolean = false): Boolean { ledger[tx.id] = "PREPARING" val prepared = mutableListOf<Action>() for (a in tx.actions) { if (!prepare(tx, a)) { prepared.forEach { items.getValue(it.key).ongoing = null; log(tx.id, "cancel ${it.key}") } ledger[tx.id] = "CANCELLED" log(tx.id, "-> cancelled; nothing was written") return false } prepared += a } ledger[tx.id] = "COMMITTING" // the decision is durable before any item changes if (crashBeforeCommit) { log(tx.id, "-> coordinator crashes after deciding COMMIT; both items stay held") return false } commit(tx) log(tx.id, "-> committed") return true } fun transfer(id: String, ts: Long, from: String, to: String, amount: Long) = Tx(id, ts, listOf(Action(from, -amount) { it >= amount }, Action(to, amount))) println("== two transfers out of A-1001 collide") val t1 = transfer("T1", 100, "A-1001", "A-2002", 3_000) // T2 moves 50.00 from A-1001 to A-3003, and happens to list the credit first val t2 = Tx("T2", 101, listOf(Action("A-3003", 5_000), Action("A-1001", -5_000) { it >= 5_000 })) // T1 prepares A-1001 first; T2 prepares A-3003, then reaches A-1001 while T1 holds it prepare(t1, t1.actions[0]) run(t2) prepare(t1, t1.actions[1]) ledger["T1"] = "COMMITTING" commit(t1) log("T1", "-> committed") println("T2 gets TransactionConflict. The SDK doesn't retry a cancelled transaction: your code does,") println("with a new timestamp and the same idempotency key, after a short backoff.") run(Tx("T2", 105, t2.actions)) println() println("== a coordinator dies between its decision and the commits") run(transfer("T3", 110, "A-2002", "A-1001", 2_000), crashBeforeCommit = true) run(transfer("T4", 111, "A-1001", "A-3003", 1_000)) println("recovery manager scans the ledger: ${ledger.filterValues { it == "COMMITTING" }.keys} decided but not completed") commit(transfer("T3", 110, "A-2002", "A-1001", 2_000)) log("T3", "-> completed by a new coordinator") run(transfer("T4", 112, "A-1001", "A-3003", 1_000)) println() println("balances: " + items.values.joinToString { "${it.key} ${it.balance}" } + " (total ${items.values.sumOf { it.balance }})") }

sections.h: MongoDB: each transaction reads a snapshot, and the first writer wins
sections.html:
The Data models track's lesson on document stores kept a payment and its refunds in one document, so one guarded updateOne could check and change them together. When the rule spans documents, say a transfer that changes two account documents and inserts a ledger document, MongoDB has multi-document transactions. They run only on a replica set or a sharded cluster, not on a standalone server; lab Compose files for this track run even a single node as a one-member replica set, rs0, for that reason.

Inside a transaction you can read, decide in Kotlin and write, like an Oracle transaction. So how does MongoDB keep two transactions apart? Build it up.

Version 1 locks everything a transaction reads, until it commits. That's two-phase locking, from lesson 5. It's correct, and a long report would block every transfer it touched.

Version 2 is what MongoDB does for reads. Each transaction reads from a snapshot: the data as committed when the transaction started. The storage engine keeps old versions for this, the multi-version idea from lesson 4. Reads never block and are never blocked.

Writes still need a rule. If two transactions change the same document, the second write fails at once with WriteConflict. First writer wins, and nobody waits. The error carries the label TransientTransactionError, which means: abort and run the whole transaction again. Retrying just the failed statement would be wrong, because the transaction's snapshot no longer matches reality. The Try-it shows tx2 failing, then retrying with a new snapshot that sees tx1's debit, at which point its own condition is false.

The Java driver's session.withTransaction { } does this loop for you. It reruns the block on TransientTransactionError, retries just the commit on UnknownTransactionCommitResult, and gives up after 120 seconds. The lab writes the same loop by hand so you know what it does.

Four limits matter in practice. A plain write outside any transaction that hits a document an open transaction has changed waits until that transaction ends. A transaction must finish within transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds, 60 seconds by default, or a cleanup task aborts it. MongoDB 9.0 also caps the number of multi-document transactions open at once from clients at 10,000 (maxConcurrentMultiDocumentTransactions); past that, a new one fails with TooManyOpenTransactions, so a pool of slow transactions can't pile up without bound. And snapshot isolation isn't serializable: two transactions that read the same two balances and each write a different one don't conflict, which is lesson 3's write skew. Keep the rule in the documents you write, with guarded updates. On a sharded cluster, a transaction that writes to several shards commits with lesson 7's two-phase protocol, coordinated by one of the shards, so it costs extra round trips. Jepsen's 2020 test of MongoDB 4.2.6, from the document stores lesson, adds one more: set readConcern: "snapshot" and writeConcern: "majority" on every transaction yourself.

try.title: Collide two transactions, then outlive the time limit
steps: From the labs folder, start MongoDB 9.0 as a one-member replica set: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml up -d --wait.
Read the script below. Predict what tx2's debit prints, what an outside read sees before tx1 commits, and what tx2 sees when it retries. The last part sleeps for 12 seconds on purpose.
Run it: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml exec mongo mongosh sfz --quiet /sfz/nosql-10-transactions.js. Then stop MongoDB: docker compose -f env/mongo.yml down -v.

Run against env/mongo.yml (a one-member replica set): // docker compose -f env/mongo.yml exec mongo mongosh sfz --quiet /sfz/nosql-10-transactions.js db.accounts.drop() db.accounts.insertMany([{ _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: 10000 }, { _id: "A-2002", balanceMinor: 5000 }]) // two sessions, two transactions, each with its own snapshot const opts = { readConcern: { level: "snapshot" }, writeConcern: { w: "majority" } } const s1 = db.getMongo().startSession(), a1 = s1.getDatabase("sfz").accounts const s2 = db.getMongo().startSession(), a2 = s2.getDatabase("sfz").accounts s1.startTransaction(opts) s2.startTransaction(opts) print("tx1 reads A-1001:", a1.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }).balanceMinor) print("tx2 reads A-1001:", a2.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }).balanceMinor) // tx1 debits 30.00 first; tx2 then tries to debit 80.00 from the same document print("tx1 debit 3000:", a1.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: { $gte: 3000 } }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: -3000 } }).modifiedCount) try { a2.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: { $gte: 8000 } }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: -8000 } }) } catch (e) { print("tx2 debit 8000:", e.codeName, JSON.stringify(e.errorLabels)) } print("outside, before tx1 commits:", db.accounts.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }).balanceMinor) a1.updateOne({ _id: "A-2002" }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: 3000 } }) s1.commitTransaction() print("outside, after tx1 commits:", db.accounts.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }).balanceMinor) // the retry is a NEW transaction with a new snapshot: it sees 7000, and its condition is false s2.abortTransaction() s2.startTransaction(opts) print("tx2 retry reads A-1001:", a2.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }).balanceMinor) print("tx2 retry debit 8000:", a2.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: { $gte: 8000 } }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: -8000 } }).modifiedCount) s2.abortTransaction() // a plain write, outside any transaction, to a document an open transaction has changed: it waits s1.startTransaction(opts) a1.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001" }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: -100 } }) let t = Date.now() try { db.runCommand({ update: "accounts", updates: [{ q: { _id: "A-1001" }, u: { $inc: { balanceMinor: -1 } } }], maxTimeMS: 2000 }) } catch (e) { print("outside write:", e.codeName, "after", Date.now() - t, "ms") } s1.abortTransaction() // the time limit: 60 seconds by default; set it to 5 to watch it, then put it back print("transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds:", db.adminCommand({ getParameter: 1, transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds: 1 }).transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds) db.adminCommand({ setParameter: 1, transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds: 5 }) s1.startTransaction(opts) a1.updateOne({ _id: "A-1001" }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: -100 } }) sleep(12000) // a slow call to the card issuer, say try { s1.commitTransaction() } catch (e) { print("commit after 12 s:", e.codeName) } db.adminCommand({ setParameter: 1, transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds: 60 }) print("A-1001 at the end:", db.accounts.findOne({ _id: "A-1001" }).balanceMinor)

tx2 reads A-1001: 10000
tx1 debit 3000: 1
tx2 debit 8000: WriteConflict ["TransientTransactionError"]
outside, before tx1 commits: 10000

Both transactions read 10000 from their snapshots. tx1 writes first, so tx2's write fails at once with WriteConflict and the label TransientTransactionError. Outside, nobody sees tx1's debit until it commits. tx2's retry is a new transaction with a new snapshot: it sees 7000, and its guarded debit of 8000 modifies nothing. The plain write outside a transaction waited for tx1 until its 2-second maxTimeMS ran out. With the limit set to 5 seconds, the transaction that slept 12 was aborted by the server's cleanup, so its commit finds NoSuchTransaction and its debit never happened: A-1001 is still 7000.

sections.h: Cassandra: Paxos agrees on one value for one partition
sections.html:
The Data models track's lesson on wide-column stores claimed an idempotency key with INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS, and the Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication showed why plain quorums can't do that. Two coordinators both read "no row" at QUORUM, both write, and last write wins keeps one of them without telling the other. A compare-and-set needs the replicas to agree on one order before anyone writes. Cassandra has no leader to decide, so it runs Paxos, Leslie Lamport's consensus protocol, for that one partition. The Consistency and consensus track builds Raft, a close relative that elects a leader first; this section builds just enough Paxos for one partition.

Build it from the race. Version 1 stamps each attempt with a ballot, a number that grows, and asks the replicas to promise to refuse anything with a lower one. Once a majority has promised ballot 2, an attempt still holding ballot 1 is refused when it tries to write. Any two majorities share a replica, so two attempts can't both hold a majority's promise.

That isn't enough. Say attempt 1 got its value accepted by one replica and then its coordinator died. Attempt 2 can't tell whether that value was already chosen. So every promise also reports any value the replica accepted but never saw committed, and Paxos's one rule says the newcomer must finish that value before proposing its own. The second stepper shows it.

Cassandra's lightweight transaction (LWT) is four round trips to a majority of replicas, all visible in the Try-it's trace:

  1. Prepare and promise: "Promising ballot".
  2. Read the current row and check the IF: "Reading existing values for CAS precondition".
  3. Propose and accept: "Accepting proposal".
  4. Commit, which writes the row into the table: "Committing proposal".

A plain write is one round trip. The Paxos state lives in a table of its own, system.paxos, which is why the trace says "Adding to paxos memtable". If the condition is false, you get [applied] = False and the current row. The Paxos phases use the serial consistency level, SERIAL or LOCAL_SERIAL, and a read at SERIAL goes through Paxos too, so it sees every applied LWT.

The cost list is short. Each LWT waits for four majority round trips; two clients racing on one partition can keep bumping each other's ballots until one gives up after cas_contention_timeout (1 second in the 5.0.9 cassandra.yaml). Cassandra 4.1 added Paxos v2, which needs two round trips for a write, but 5.0.9 still ships paxos_variant: v1 as the default; switching takes a full repair and a rolling restart. And it's one partition only: a batch with an IF condition can't span partitions.

try.title: Trace a plain insert and two lightweight transactions
steps: Start Cassandra from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait (one to two minutes), then open docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh.

sections.h: Accord in 6.0, and when a better model beats a transaction
sections.html:
Cassandra 6.0 adds Accord: transactions across partitions and tables, strict serializable, with no leader. Any node can coordinate, and the common case needs one round trip of consensus. As of November 2026 it's still alpha. The Docker image cassandra:6.0-alpha2 exists, the Apache downloads page still lists 5.0 as the newest released line, 6.0 has no release date yet, and the syntax may change before release. Accord also needs Cassandra's new cluster metadata service, which an upgraded cluster switches on with nodetool cms initialize, a step that is not easily undone. In the alpha, Accord is off until accord.enabled: true is set in cassandra.yaml, and each table opts in with transactional_mode = 'full'. A transaction reads with LET, decides with IF ... THEN, and writes, between BEGIN TRANSACTION and COMMIT TRANSACTION. The Try-it moves 30.00 between two partitions of two tables in one statement. Treat it as the direction Cassandra is going, not something to build payments on yet. Systems built for transactions from the start take the other road: the Consistency and consensus track's lesson on distributed SQL shows how Spanner and CockroachDB run lesson 7's two-phase commit over participants that are each replicated with consensus.

Now the harder question: when should you not use a transaction at all? Every tool in this lesson charges something. DynamoDB bills two writes per item and cancels on contention. MongoDB aborts on write conflicts and after 60 seconds. A Cassandra LWT costs four round trips per write. And across services, which is where most of your transfers really run, there's no shared transaction at all.

A better data model often removes the need:

  • Put what must change together into one item or document. The document stores lesson's refunds array made the refund rule a single guarded update.
  • Make one conditional write do the job. An idempotency claim is one attribute_not_exists put or one IF NOT EXISTS, not a transaction.
  • Split a cross-account transfer into steps that are each atomic on one partition, and let a durable workflow drive them to the end: debit A-1001 and record the pending transfer in A-1001's own document, then credit A-2002 idempotently, then mark it done. If the credit can never succeed, a compensating step refunds the debit. That's lesson 7's saga. Money is visibly "in flight" for a moment, and a reconciliation report can find any transfer that got stuck.

For a transfer between two accounts that the business already treats as pending, use the saga, in a Temporal workflow like the ones in the Encoding, APIs and workflows track's lesson on durable execution. Use a transaction when the invariant needs one indivisible step, such as an idempotency claim and the payment it guards, and keep that transaction inside one partition or one document when you can.

     A-2002 |     txf-k-1 |         3000

(2 rows)

The first transaction read 10000, the condition held, and all four writes landed together, on two partitions of balances and two of ledger. The second read 7000, its condition was false, and none of its writes happened. cqlsh also prints a warning that it was built against 6.0-alpha2 while the server calls itself 6.0, one more sign this is a preview.

MongoDB: transactions, and why data modeling comes first

analogy: A cross-partition transaction works like a travel agent booking a flight and a hotel for one trip. She first asks each to hold the booking: once held, the seat can't go to anyone else, and the airline has promised to confirm it if asked. Only when both holds are in place does she write "confirmed" in her file and tell both. DynamoDB's twist is that a seat already held for another trip makes the airline say no at once instead of keeping a waiting list, and her file is kept where any colleague can pick up the booking if she goes home sick. Paxos is booking the last seat when there is no agent at all: anyone may try, the request with the newest ticket number goes first, and a newcomer who finds a half-recorded booking must finish recording it before trying their own. The analogy breaks on time: a hotel hold lasts a day, while all of this must finish in milliseconds, and a conflict means the whole trip is cancelled and booked again from the start.
world: Your Oracle transfers are one local transaction, and an XA transaction across Oracle and a message queue is lesson 7's two-phase commit with a coordinator in the application server, which is why a crashed JTA coordinator can leave in-doubt transactions for a DBA to resolve. Moving to NoSQL changes where that coordinator lives, not whether you need one. For a wallet in DynamoDB, keep the debit, the ledger entry and the idempotency claim in one TransactWriteItems, and expect TransactionConflict on a busy merchant account; retry with jitter and the same client token, and don't build a report on a Query that could see half a transaction. In MongoDB, use withTransaction and set snapshot and majority on it. For a transfer between two services, there is no shared transaction: model it as a saga in a Temporal workflow, with each step one atomic, idempotent write keyed by the transfer id from the Kafka command.
mistake: The most common mistake is wrapping a read-then-write in a transaction and assuming the transaction makes it safe, then retrying only the statement that failed. In MongoDB the read came from a snapshot, so when the write fails with WriteConflict the decision you made from that read is stale; rerunning just the write either fails again or applies a decision based on old data. In DynamoDB the read was never part of the transaction at all. People do it because a transaction feels like a lock around everything inside it. The fix: put the condition in the write itself (a guarded update or a condition expression), and on TransientTransactionError or TransactionConflict rerun the whole unit of work, reads included, with the same idempotency key.

a.label: MongoDB: withTransaction
a.title: MongoDB Java driver, from Kotlin
a.html: client.startSession().use { session -> val options = TransactionOptions.builder() .readConcern(ReadConcern.SNAPSHOT).writeConcern(WriteConcern.MAJORITY).build() // the block may run several times: on TransientTransactionError it is retried session.withTransaction({ val from = accounts.find(session, eq("_id", "A-1001")).first()!! // read from the snapshot require(from.getLong("balanceMinor") >= 3_000) { "insufficient" } // decide in Kotlin accounts.updateOne(session, and(eq("_id", "A-1001"), gte("balanceMinor", 3_000L)), inc("balanceMinor", -3_000L)) accounts.updateOne(session, eq("_id", "A-2002"), inc("balanceMinor", 3_000L)) ledger.insertOne(session, Document("_id", "txf-k-1").append("amountMinor", 3_000L)) }, options) }

b.label: Cassandra 6.0 alpha: Accord
b.title: CQL, syntax may change before release
b.html: BEGIN TRANSACTION LET src = (SELECT balance_minor FROM payments.balances WHERE account_id = 'A-1001'); IF src.balance_minor >= 3000 THEN UPDATE payments.balances SET balance_minor -= 3000 WHERE account_id = 'A-1001'; UPDATE payments.balances SET balance_minor += 3000 WHERE account_id = 'A-2002'; INSERT INTO payments.ledger (account_id, transfer_id, amount_minor) VALUES ('A-1001', 'txf-k-1', -3000); END IF COMMIT TRANSACTION;

compare.note: MongoDB runs a conversation: the session opens a snapshot, your Kotlin reads and decides, and the server checks for write conflicts as the writes arrive. The flexibility costs a retry loop around your own code, which withTransaction provides. Accord takes the whole transaction as one statement: reads go in LET, decisions in IF, and the cluster orders it against every other transaction before running it, so there is no conflict for your code to retry. DynamoDB's TransactWriteItems sits between them: one request, but with no reads at all, only conditions. Because MongoDB lets your code decide between the read and the write, keep the condition in the update's filter as well, as the Kotlin does; the other two decide inside the database.

worked.title: A transfer between two accounts without a cross-partition transaction

steps.say: Start from the requirement and what the business already accepts. A transfer may show as pending for a few seconds; it must never move money twice or lose it. The two accounts are two MongoDB documents, possibly on two shards.
steps.code:
transfer txf-k-1: 30.00 from A-1001 to A-2002
must hold:  never debited twice, never credited twice, never debited without a credit in the end
may happen: A-1001 shows the debit a moment before A-2002 shows the credit

steps.say: Step 1 is one atomic write on A-1001's document: debit it and record the pending transfer inside it. The filter checks the balance AND that this transfer id isn't recorded yet, so a retry modifies nothing.
steps.code: db.accounts.updateOne( { _id: "A-1001", balanceMinor: { $gte: 3000 }, "pending.id": { $ne: "txf-k-1" } }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: -3000 }, $push: { pending: { id: "txf-k-1", to: "A-2002", amountMinor: 3000 } } }) // modifiedCount 0: insufficient funds, or already done; read the document to tell which

steps.say: Step 2 is one atomic write on A-2002's document: credit it, guarded by the same transfer id, so running it twice credits once.
steps.code: db.accounts.updateOne( { _id: "A-2002", "credited": { $ne: "txf-k-1" } }, { $inc: { balanceMinor: 3000 }, $push: { credited: "txf-k-1" } })

steps.say: Step 3 closes the transfer on A-1001: move it from pending to done. If step 2 can never succeed (the account was closed), the compensating step refunds A-1001 instead, guarded the same way.
steps.code: db.accounts.updateOne( { _id: "A-1001", "pending.id": "txf-k-1" }, { $pull: { pending: { id: "txf-k-1" } }, $push: { done: "txf-k-1" } }) // compensation, instead of step 2 and 3: // { _id: "A-1001", "pending.id": "txf-k-1" } -> $inc +3000, $pull the pending entry

steps.say: Something has to run steps 1 to 3 to the end, through crashes and deploys. That is a durable workflow, from the Encoding, APIs and workflows track's lesson on durable execution: a Temporal workflow whose activities are these three writes, each safe to retry because each is guarded by the transfer id.
steps.code:
workflow transfer(txf-k-1):
  debit(A-1001)           activity, retried until it answers: done / insufficient
  credit(A-2002)          activity, retried; on permanent failure -> refund(A-1001)
  close(A-1001)           activity, retried
# no step ever holds two documents at once; a crash resumes at the next step

steps.say: Count what you traded. No transaction, so no write conflicts across accounts, no 60-second limit and no two-phase cost. In return: three writes instead of one commit, a moment where the money is visibly in flight, and a workflow engine you must run. For payments that is usually the right trade, because pending already exists in the business.
steps.code:
one transaction           saga of single-document writes
atomic across docs     yes                       no: in flight for a moment
conflicts / retries    the whole transaction     each step on its own
needs                  a replica set, 60 s max   a workflow engine (Temporal)
works across services  no                        yes

steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. PaxosRegisterTest needs no Docker; MongoTransfersTest starts a one-member MongoDB replica set through Testcontainers (a few seconds, more on the first pull). All fourteen fail.
In PaxosRegister.kt, write Acceptor.prepare and Acceptor.accept. Each is three lines: compare the ballot with promised, then remember. The first two tests pass.

Write compareAndSet from its KDoc: majority check, prepare, finish any unfinished proposal and start again, read, propose, commit, counting round trips. Seven more pass, including the one where a crashed proposer's value must win and the one that races 300 rounds of claims with lost messages.

In MongoTransfers.kt, write transfer: one session, a loop of startTransaction(options), the ledger insert, the guarded debit, the credit and the commit, with a retry on TransientTransactionError. Five more pass. The conflict test holds a rival transaction open on A-1001 for 300 ms and expects your first attempts to fail and a later one to succeed.
hints: prepare: val p = promised; if (p != null && ballot <= p) return Promise.Rejected(p), then set promised and return Promise.Ok(inProgress, committed). accept refuses only when proposal.ballot < promised (equal is fine: it's the proposer that prepared).

In compareAndSet, keep var trips = 0 outside a while (true) loop and continue after finishing someone else's proposal. Unfinished means: an inProgress whose ballot is greater than the highest committed ballot among the Ok replies.
highestPromise(replicas) gives the ballot for Contended. read(replicas) is the read step.
Mongo: every call takes the session first: accounts.updateOne(session, filter, update). A duplicate ledger id is a MongoWriteException with e.error.category == ErrorCategory.DUPLICATE_KEY.

Catch MongoException, call abortQuietly(session), and if e.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL) sleep backoff(attempt) and loop. For the commit, loop while the error has UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION_COMMIT_RESULT_LABEL.

drill.title: The transaction retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. In Kotlin, write the loop that runs a MongoDB transaction body with the core API: start a session, start a transaction with snapshot and majority, run body(session), commit, and retry the whole thing on TransientTransactionError (up to 10 attempts) and only the commit on UnknownTransactionCommitResult. Then say in one sentence why retrying just the failed statement is wrong.

answer.html: fun <T> inTransaction(client: MongoClient, body: (ClientSession) -> T): T { val options = TransactionOptions.builder() .readConcern(ReadConcern.SNAPSHOT).writeConcern(WriteConcern.MAJORITY).build() client.startSession().use { session -> var attempt = 0 while (true) { attempt++ session.startTransaction(options) // a fresh snapshot every attempt try { val result = body(session) while (true) { // retry ONLY the commit if its outcome is unknown try { session.commitTransaction(); break } catch (e: MongoException) { if (!e.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.UNKNOWN_TRANSACTION_COMMIT_RESULT_LABEL)) throw e } } return result } catch (e: MongoException) { if (session.hasActiveTransaction()) session.abortTransaction() if (!e.hasErrorLabel(MongoException.TRANSIENT_TRANSACTION_ERROR_LABEL) || attempt == 10) throw e Thread.sleep(10L * attempt) // back off, then rerun reads AND writes } } } } // Retrying one statement is wrong: the transaction's earlier reads came from a snapshot that a // conflicting commit has made stale, so every decision taken from them has to be taken again.

recap: Lesson 7's rule holds in NoSQL too: across partitions, every participant first promises, one decision is recorded durably, then everything changes. One item, document or partition is atomic for free because one node owns it.

DynamoDB: up to 100 items and 4 MB in one Region. Coordinators prepare each item (condition, timestamp, nobody else in flight) and record decisions in a replicated ledger. A rejected prepare is TransactionConflict; nothing waits, so retry with the same token. Query and Scan read transactions as read committed.

MongoDB: multi-document transactions read a snapshot and let the first writer of a document win; the loser gets WriteConflict with TransientTransactionError and reruns the whole transaction. 60 seconds by default, and 9.0 caps open transactions at 10,000. Set snapshot and majority yourself.
Cassandra 5.0: a lightweight transaction runs Paxos on one partition, four round trips in the default v1 against one for a plain write. A newcomer must finish any accepted value it finds.

Accord in Cassandra 6.0 adds strict serializable transactions across partitions, still alpha in November 2026. Before reaching for any transaction, try one document, one conditional write, or a saga of single-partition steps.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "NoSQL has transactions now, so can we just wrap the transfer in one and stop worrying?" Explain what a transaction across partitions has to do, what each of DynamoDB, MongoDB and Cassandra does when two writers collide, and when you'd model the transfer differently.
explain.answer: Across partitions no single machine can make the change atomic, so every store does a version of the same thing: each participant first promises (DynamoDB holds the item after a successful prepare, Paxos replicas promise a ballot), one decision is recorded where a crash can't lose it (DynamoDB's ledger, a majority of Paxos replicas), and only then does data change. Collisions are where they differ. DynamoDB rejects the second transaction's prepare and cancels it with TransactionConflict; our code retries with backoff. MongoDB gives each transaction a snapshot and fails the second writer of a document with WriteConflict, labelled TransientTransactionError, so we rerun the whole transaction, reads included; it also aborts anything older than 60 seconds. Cassandra only offers compare-and-set on one partition, a lightweight transaction that costs four Paxos round trips, and Accord for multi-partition transactions is still alpha in 6.0. So transactions exist, but they cost writes, retries and latency, and none spans services. For a transfer between two accounts I'd rather do two single-document conditional writes keyed by the transfer id, a debit that records the pending transfer and an idempotent credit, driven by a Temporal workflow with a compensating refund. I'd keep a transaction for things that must be one step, like an idempotency claim and the payment it guards, ideally inside one partition.

deeper.html:
DynamoDB's paper describes more tricks than this lesson used. Single reads aren't blocked by a prepared transaction: a GetItem returns the last committed value and is ordered before the pending transaction. A plain PutItem with no condition can even be ordered before a prepared transaction, because the transaction's later write will overwrite it anyway. TransactGetItems is "writeless": it reads every item with its log sequence number, reads them again, and succeeds only if nothing changed in between, so a read transaction never writes anything. And items that were deleted are tracked with one maximum-delete timestamp per partition rather than a tombstone per item, which occasionally cancels a transaction that could have run.

Compare the three answers to lesson 7's in-doubt problem. Classic two-phase commit keeps the decision on one coordinator's disk, so its participants block when it dies. DynamoDB keeps the decision in a replicated ledger and lets any coordinator finish it. Google Spanner goes further: every participant is itself a Paxos group, so a participant never disappears either; the Consistency and consensus track's lesson on distributed SQL takes that apart.

Cassandra's Paxos v2 (4.1 and later) cuts a write to two round trips, by combining the read with the prepare and the commit with the next operation's prepare, roughly. The cassandra.yaml of 5.0.9 lists the variants with their round trips: v1 "Expect 4RTs for a write and 3RTs for a read", v2 "Expect 2RTs for a write, and either 1RT or 2RT for a read". To switch, run a full repair on every node, set paxos_variant: v2 and restart node by node; going back is just as simple.

Notice that Accord's "one round trip in the common case" is a fast path: when replicas agree on the transaction's place in the order straight away, it commits in one round; when concurrent transactions disagree, it falls back to a slower path. That's the same shape as Paxos with a stable leader, and the reason contention costs latency in every one of these systems.

If you want to read one more paper, read Jepsen's MongoDB 4.2.6 report end to end. It shows how a test harness finds lost writes and read skew, and why a database's defaults and its documentation matter as much as its protocol.
